characterization_methods.key_findings: 19Al alloy aged at 600 °C for 3 h: 899.8 ± 6.8 HV
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: load 9.8 N, dwell 15 s; 5 repeated measurements averaged per sample
characterization_methods.purpose: measure the Vickers hardness of the aged samples

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: GeminiSEM 300 SEM; scanning step size 1.5 μm (low magnification) and 0.05 μm (high magnification)
characterization_methods.key_findings: Fig 6(b): the phase map is almost entirely green β-Mn (100 μm scale bar); the magnified phase map (b2, 5 μm) shows small violet particles labelled 'New FCC phase' within β-Mn; the IPF map shows many differently coloured grains.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: electrolytically polished samples (10 % perchloric acid + 90 % ethanol)
characterization_methods.purpose: identify the phase constitution and microstructure of the 19Al alloy after aging at 600 °C for 3 h

interfaces.interface_notes: The intrinsic hardness of the FCC Cu-rich and BCC precipitates at the β-Mn interfaces is lower than that of β-Mn; their content increases with Al content.
interfaces.phase_evolution: α → α + FCC Cu-rich phase → α-Mn + β-Mn + BCC phase → β-Mn + BCC phase + FCC Cu-rich phase. For the 19Al alloy, at 600 °C the α matrix had almost completely transformed into β-Mn after just 1 h of aging, with numerous fine precipitates (BCC and FCC) distributed within the β-Mn.

processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Alloy ingots with nominal composition Fe-35Mn-19Al-5Cu (at.%) were produced by melting high-purity (>99.9 %) raw materials in a vacuum induction furnace under an argon atmosphere; the alloy is referred to as 19Al.
The ingots were homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h.
Hot-rolled into plates with a thickness of 4 mm.
Plates were cut into 10 × 5 × 2 mm³ samples using electrical discharge machining for Vickers hardness measurements and microstructure characterizations.
Samples were solution treated at 1100 °C for 10 min under an argon atmosphere, followed by oil quenching. This is the parent process (proc_st-1100c-10min-oq).
Solution-treated samples were aged at temperatures between 525 °C and 650 °C for 1, 3, 6 and 10 h, followed by water quenching. This sample corresponds to the 600 °C / 3 h condition.

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Vickers hardness measured with an HVS-1000 digital microhardness tester, load 9.8 N, dwell 15 s; each sample tested 5 times and reported as the average.

phases_present.morphology: matrix phase; α matrix almost completely transformed into β-Mn (EBSD phase map almost entirely green)
small particles at β-Mn interfaces (magnified EBSD shows small violet particles labelled 'New FCC phase')

structures.overall_structure: After aging the 19Al alloy at 600 °C for 3 h, the α matrix had almost completely transformed into β-Mn; the EBSD phase map is almost entirely green β-Mn, with fine new precipitates (FCC Cu-rich and BCC phases) distributed at the β-Mn interfaces. The magnified EBSD phase map shows small violet 'New FCC phase' particles within β-Mn.

unmapped_findings: The nanoindentation, intrinsic β-Mn hardness, β-Mn composition, and fracture-toughness measurements in the paper were performed on the 'hardest samples' of each alloy; for the 19Al alloy the hardest condition is 600 °C for 10 h (peak Vickers hardness 917.8 HV), NOT the 600 °C/3 h sample extracted here. Therefore nanoindentation average hardness 10.4 ± 1.3 GPa, intrinsic β-Mn hardness 12.5 ± 0.4 GPa, KIC = 3.5 MPa·m^1/2 with average crack length 35 μm, and β-Mn composition (Mn 36.2 at.%, Al 17.5 at.%, Cu 2.6 at.%) cannot be attributed to the 600 °C/3 h sample.

For the 19Al alloy, only a small amount of β-Mn (12.1 %) precipitated after aging at 525 °C for 10 h, resulting in a minimal increase in hardness (this is a different aging condition than the 600 °C/3 h sample).
For the 19Al alloy aged at 650 °C for 6 h, the volume fraction of FCC Cu-rich and BCC precipitates reached 6.5 % and its Vickers hardness was only 810.9 HV (different aging condition).
The XRD measurements were performed on 19Al aged at 550 °C for 6 h (both α-Mn and β-Mn peaks present), not on the 600 °C/3 h sample.
The 19Al alloy reached its peak (917.8 HV) after aging at 600 °C for 10 h; the optimal aging temperature range to achieve ultra-high hardness for the 19Al alloy was 575–625 °C.
The 19Al alloy's α→β-Mn transformation completes only after 10 h at 550 °C, and at 600 °C and above within about 1 h; the increase in Al content slowed down the β-Mn precipitation kinetics.
